MCP4725
12-Bit Digital-to-Analog Converter with EEPROM Memory
Features

• 12-Bit Resolution
• On-Board Nonvolatile Memory (EEPROM)
• ±0.2 LSB DNL (typical)
• External A0 Address Pin
• Normal or Power-Down Mode
• Fast Settling Time: 6 µs (typical)
• External Voltage Reference $( \mathsf { V _ { D D } } )$
• Rail-to-Rail Output
• Low Power Consumption
• Single-Supply Operation: 2.7V to 5.5V
• I<sup>2</sup>C Interface:
- Eight Available Addresses
- Standard (100 kbps), Fast (400 kbps), and High-Speed (3.4 Mbps) Modes
• Small 6-Lead SOT-23 and DFN Package Options
• Extended Temperature Range: $- 4 0 ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C }$ to $+ 1 2 5 ^ { \circ } C$
Applications

• Set Point or Offset Trimming
• Sensor Calibration
• Closed-Loop Servo Control
• Low Power Portable Instrumentation
• PC Peripherals
• Data Acquisition Systems

General Description

The MCP4725 is a low-power, high accuracy, single channel, 12-bit buffered voltage output Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) with nonvolatile memory (EEPROM). Its on-board precision output amplifier allows it to achieve rail-to-rail analog output swing.

The DAC input and configuration data can be programmed to the nonvolatile memory (EEPROM) by the user using $1 ^ { 2 } \mathsf { C }$ interface command. The nonvolatile memory feature enables the DAC device to hold the DAC input code during power-off time, and the DAC output is available immediately after power-up. This feature is very useful when the DAC device is used as a supporting device for other devices in the network.

The device includes a Power-on-Reset (POR) circuit to ensure reliable power-up and an on-board charge pump for the EEPROM programming voltage. The DAC reference is driven from $\nabla _ { \mathsf { D D } }$ directly. In powerdown mode, the output amplifier can be configured to present a known low, medium, or high resistance output load.
The MCP4725 has an external A0 address bit selection pin. This A0 pin can be tied to $\nabla _ { \mathrm { D D } }$ or $\nabla _ { \mathrm { S S } }$ of the user’s application board.
The MCP4725 has a two-wire $1 ^ { 2 } \mathbb { C }$ compatible serial interface for standard (100 kHz), fast (400 kHz), or high speed (3.4 MHz) mode.
The MCP4725 is an ideal DAC device where design simplicity and small footprint is desired, and for applications requiring the DAC device settings to be saved during power-off time.
The device is available in a small 6-pin SOT-23 and DFN package.

MCP4725
4.0 TERMINOLOGY
4.1 Resolution
The resolution is the number of DAC output states that divide the full scale range. For the 12-bit DAC, the resolution is $2 ^ { 1 2 }$ or the DAC code ranges from 0 to 4095.
4.2 LSB
The least significant bit or the ideal voltage difference between two successive codes.
EQUATION 4-1:
L S B _ {I d e a l} = \frac {V _ {R E F}}{2 ^ {n}} = \frac {(V _ {F u l l S c a l e} - V _ {Z e r o S c a l e})}{2 ^ {n} - 1}
Where:

\begin{array}{r c l} V _ {R E F} & = & \text {The reference voltage} = V _ {D D} \text {in the} \\ & & \text {MCP4725. This V_{REF} is the ideal} \\ & & \text {full scale voltage range} \\ n & = & \text {The number of digital input bits.} \\ & & (n = 1 2 \text {for MCP4725}) \end{array}
4.3 Integral Nonlinearity (INL) or Relative Accuracy

INL error is the maximum deviation between an actual code transition point and its corresponding ideal transition point (straight line). Figure 2-5 shows the INL curve of the MCP4725. The end-point method is used for the calculation. The INL error at a given input DAC code is calculated as:
EQUATION 4-2:
I N L = \frac {\left(V _ {O U T} - V _ {I d e a l}\right)}{L S B}
Where:
\begin{array}{r c l} \mathrm{V} _ {\text {Ideal}} & = & \text {Code*LSB} \\ \mathrm{V} _ {\text {OUT}} & = & \text {The output voltage measured at} \\ & & \text {the given input code} \end{array}
4.4 Differential Nonlinearity (DNL)

Differential nonlinearity error (Figure 4-2) is the measure of step size between codes in actual transfer function. The ideal step size between codes is 1 LSB. A DNL error of zero would imply that every code is exactly 1 LSB wide. If the DNL error is less than 1 LSB, the DAC guarantees monotonic output and no missing codes. The DNL error between any two adjacent codes is calculated as follows:
EQUATION 4-3:
D N L = \frac {\Delta V _ {O U T} - L S B}{L S B}
Where:
\begin{array}{r l r} \Delta V _ {\text {OUT}} & = & \text {The measured DAC output} \\ & & \text {voltage difference between two} \\ & & \text {adjacent input codes.} \end{array}
